questions.prompt: Informal fallacies, as Hicks defines them here, are mistakes in reasoning where:
choices: A The premises seem to support the conclusion but actually provide no support.
B Every informal remark is automatically valid.
C Only categorical syllogisms can go wrong.
D Emotions have been successfully banned from life.
questions.explain: They look like support from premises to conclusion, but the support isn’t there—fallacious, and “informal” because they show up across forms of reasoning.

questions.prompt: Subjectivism in its crude form, on this lecture’s account, is:
choices: A I want X to be true, so I will believe X is true.
B I gather evidence first, then decide what I want.
C I always go to the doctor when symptoms appear.
D I treat emotions as the organ of truth.
questions.explain: Standard form: I want X true; therefore I believe X. The “evidence” is just one’s wanting.

questions.prompt: The appeal to majority is a fallacy, Hicks says, primarily because:
choices: A Crowds never share any true beliefs.
B Other people’s believing X, by itself, does not tell you whether X is true.
C History shows majorities are always right.
D Asch proved visual acuity is impossible.
questions.explain: You don’t have their reasoning. “Many believe X, therefore I believe X” is a failure of independent judgment.

questions.prompt: Ad hominem, as Hicks explains the Latin label that stuck, is:
choices: A Attacking the person (or the person-as-speaker) instead of the argument or ideas.
B Citing Aristotle as an authority on biology.
C Affirming the consequent in a hypothetical syllogism.
D Defining a square in geometry.
questions.explain: Instead of attacking the argument/ideas, you attack the person.

questions.prompt: The crude ad hominem pattern Hicks writes as a schema is:
choices: A X says Y; X has some disliked trait; therefore Y is false.
B X says Y; therefore Y is true because X is famous.
C If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q (and that is valid).
D All S are P; some P are Q; therefore gossip is evidence.
questions.explain: X says Y is true, but X is [insult]; therefore Y is false—the person’s disliked feature is treated as refuting the claim.
